review_text: I'd give 4.7 stars if PlanetTerp had such an option. This is a hard class. Not in the way that MATH140/141 are considered "hard", or in the way that Kruskal's classes are "hard" (at least his 351), but rather it is hard by virtue of the material. Algorithms are just often difficult concepts to grasp and really understand to the depth that Childs' wants his students to be able to grasp and understand for his assignments and exams. The class is paced quite nicely for me - I showed up to every lecture, and I feel like I gained something from each one. I was able to ask questions pretty frequently (perhaps too frequently), and Childs' would always spend the time to think about an answer to each one, and I felt that that helped me understand the material greatly. He records all of his lectures and posts all of his notes. The only things from class not available asynchronously online are the Q&A times that he holds in the 5-10 minutes before each class begins. The assignments are hard. (Did I mention the class is hard?) The first two took me about 10 hours each, and the other three 15-20 hours each. Each one is a set of five problems, the answers to which require (unless you're a super-mega-genius I guess) intuition and material from the lectures. A quote from one of his office hours: "If you're stuck on this problem, think about the algorithms we covered in class; I make the homeworks directly related [to those]." - Childs My strategy for the homeworks were to look at the problems when they were assigned, then keep them in mind over the next two weeks of lectures (each assignment is assigned exactly two weeks before they're due). Spending the time to actually understand the material on them is definitely helpful - they're actually harder than the exam questions by a solid margin, and they mirror the exam structure. Also, he drops the lowest of the five assignments, so each of your best four assignments comprise 10% of your final grade. Considering that there is ample time for each one, it's definitely possible to have the assignments be the grade fallback. The exams are hard. (yes.) The midterm is worth 20% of your final grade, and the final 40%. There's definitely a time-crunch aspect to this. As of writing this review, I haven't taken the final yet. But speaking from the midterm experience, there wasn't a single student that left the exam room early (shocker). Although it seemed like most of the class felt pretty bad about the midterm, to Childs', the midterm was "on the easier side." (Avg 69, median 70 iirc) I did well enough not to have major complaints about it, and other reviews go more in-depth. The textbook is... something that I didn't read. I'm sure it was useful to those who did, but the lectures + questions + office hours + assignments prepared me well enough to face the exams. Although Childs' is a great lecturer and all-around smart guy, he's definitely a bit hard to talk to. He feels like a classic computer-focused guy (which is fair, since he's getting paid for it lol), and I definitely agree with the previous reviewer that said it felt impossible to build rapport with him. TL;DR: Great lecturer, fair class, hard af so look at the grade distr. to make your choice
evidence_snippet: other three 15-20 hours each
label_rationale: Homework and exams are very difficult and time-intensive, but closely aligned with lectures and described as fair.

But you can't just not show up to lecture, there are graded in class group activities which are also useless and I'm 99% sure you could pass comfortably with an A even if you didn't get those points. There are times where an actual new or interesting concept will be introduced in lecture but more often than not you will walk away wondering what you actually learned in that 50 minute period. As for coursework the bulk of the grade comes from 4 exams, one of which is dropped. Most of them are relatively easy if you have any programming experience at all but there's a few questions that are about very specific techniques in python. The 3 homeworks throughout the semester are sort of the projects you would expect of a programming course which aside from the final project are the most time consuming. But even then if you have any programming experience at all you could finish one in 1 or 2 hours and you have unlimited attempts so you can just keep debugging and resubmitting until you check all the boxes which is nice. Considering this is the main programming course of the info sci major, I can't say this course had the rigor I expected. Maybe that sounds great to some of you but if you're expecting a programming course that has any difficulty then this is not it. Even the final project felt like a softball and the hardest part was getting your group members to commit and push to github. Most of the other assignments are just you explaining certain concepts in your own words and then provide working examples yourself which I find would be unhelpful to anyone learning python for the first time. And everyone else talking about the grading is not making it up. I kid you not, I waited until a few days before final grades were due and I got everything graded all at once in the span of an hour. So don't expect to get any grades back throughout the semester or know what your grade is at all. Overall the course structure felt really unorganized and most of the assignments weren't all that helpful aside from the homework's and group project. I'd recommend him if you have a decent understanding of python so you can just coast through the class without too much concern because if you are trying to learn python from this course, you're in for a rough time.
evidence_snippet: Most of the content you will learn are asynchronous
label_rationale: Students largely learn asynchronously, while grading and course structure are very disorganized.

review_text: This may be the worst course I've taken at UMD. The material is artificially made 20x more confusing than it is (and it's already pretty confusing) by Dr. Yoon's disorganized, scattered lecture style. I never knew how topics were connected or how they related to each other or how they fit into the bigger picture of the course. We were given maybe 1-2 examples of problems to solve for each topic (if that), but most of the exams were problem solving variations of topics we had not seen examples for. We were similarly expected to solve homeworks entirely on our own with no peer help, when we had never seen examples of those problems before in lecture or otherwise. And this would be fine if the problems were straightforward, but he usually throws in a little curveball that completely changes the entire approach to the question. And then, on top of all that, he teases us by saying the homework problems and exam problems will seem "so simple" when we see the solutions. It was infuriating every time. You will likely pass the course if you take it, because he curves. But you will waste a whole 4xx level on material that was so poorly conveyed that you'll forget it all in a month. Avoid if you can.

review_text: NORA BURKHAUSER: A generous lecturer with an energetic attitude at 9 AM. Is willing to help you learn the concepts and review for the final, and prioritizes student well-being. We even got CMSC 132 stickers :) LECTURES (Rating: 3/5): The PowerPoints were somewhat helpful in teaching us the conceptual stuff behind OOP, as that is what is mostly covered on the exam, and the review for the final was okay. It would’ve been nice to slow down or go over things more in depth, as several topics were rushed. But I do like that the lectures are recorded (especially for a 9 AM lecture), so missing one isn’t the end of the world! DISCUSSIONS (Rating: 5/5): Discussions depend on your TA. My TA was chill and went over important concepts that are needed for the projects and exams. We also had review sessions in discussion before lecture tests. HOMEWORK (Rating: 5/5): The homework assignments in this class are the programming projects. When I took 132 there were nine. If you put the time into them and learn how to implement what is needed you will succeed. One of the projects involves you working with a partner. I had a wonderful partner for that project. QUIZZES AND LABS (Rating: 4/5): The labs are free grades, so I can’t complain. You just need to try. For quizzes, Prof. B. allows you to bring a sheet of notes into the quiz - not only does this help you study but can also give you some help if you’re stuck. Some quizzes were tricky. EXAMS (Rating: 2/5): They’re okay, but they need to be shorter or there needs to be more time (50 minutes isn’t enough). I also find it weird how you handwrite code in a computer science class when in reality you type code. Do mock exams in your dorms (lucky you if you have them) to make sure you master the pacing of the questions. OVERALL RATING: 3.8/5 Structure for Fall 2025: - Programming Projects (26%; distributed across nine) - Quizzes (2.5% each; top four are graded with six given) - Labs (3%; graded for completion, top 3 graded with seven given) - Exams (12%, 14%, and 15% respectively) - Final Exam (20%)
